course.title: Caching
course.description: Every fast system you have used is a slow system with a cache in front of it. Your CPU has three levels of them, your browser has one, the CDN has one at the edge, the API gateway has one, the service keeps a Caffeine map in its heap, and Redis sits between the service and Postgres. Caching is the cheapest performance win in system design and the most common source of "but I already fixed that, why does the page still show the old value?" This module builds the moving parts in memory, one file each, so you can see exactly where the bugs hide before you meet them in Redis.

lessons.title: Caching
lessons.explanation:
# 09 · Caching

Every fast system you have used is a slow system with a cache in front of
it. Your CPU has three levels of them, your browser has one, the CDN has
one at the edge, the API gateway has one, the service keeps a Caffeine map
in its heap, and Redis sits between the service and Postgres. Caching is
the cheapest performance win in system design and the most common source
of "but I already fixed that, why does the page still show the old value?"
This module builds the moving parts in memory, one file each, so you can
see exactly where the bugs hide before you meet them in Redis.

This is the first module of the **System Design** block (09–13). The style
changes a little from 01–08: each exercise is a small in-process model of
a production idea. The Java is still plain; the point is the *behaviour*,
and the tests pin it down to the millisecond.

## The mental model

### 1 · A cache is a bet on locality

```
   request ──► cache ──hit──► answer            (microseconds)
                 │
                miss
                 ▼
              database ──► answer + remember    (milliseconds)
```

The bet: what was asked for recently (temporal locality) or often
(frequency) will be asked for again. The number that tells you whether the
bet pays is the **hit rate**, `hits / (hits + misses)`. A 99 % hit rate
means the database sees 1 request in 100; a 50 % hit rate means you added
a network hop to half your requests for a 2x saving. Measure it (04).

### 2 · Memory is finite: something must leave

Three questions decide every cache: *how big*, *who leaves when it's
full*, and *how long may an answer live*.

| policy | evicts | good at | fooled by | seen in |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LRU | least recently used | recency-heavy traffic | one big scan flushes it | Memcached, `LinkedHashMap` |
| LFU | least frequently used | stable hot set | newcomers struggle; old fame lingers | Redis `allkeys-lfu` |
| TTL | anything older than *t* | bounded staleness | nothing: it is a freshness rule, not a size rule | every HTTP `max-age` |
| W-TinyLFU | rarely-seen newcomers | mixed workloads | (state of the art) | Caffeine |

Size rules and freshness rules combine: a real cache is "LRU, max 10 000
entries, each entry at most 5 minutes old" (06).

```java
new LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) {          // true = access order
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> e) {
        return size() > capacity;                    // an LRU cache in 4 lines
    }
};
```

### 3 · Writes are where caches lie

The cache is a *copy*. The database is the truth. On every write you must
decide what happens to the copy:

| policy | on write | next read | risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cache-aside (lazy) | write db, **delete** cache key | miss → reload | one extra load per write |
| write-through | write db, **set** cache key | hit | caches values nobody reads |
| write-behind | set cache, write db later | hit | lose writes if the cache dies |

Two rules hold for all of them: **the database goes first** (if it fails,
the cache must still agree with it), and **prefer delete to set** when two
writers may race, because a delete can only cost a reload while a late set
can pin an old value forever (03).

### 4 · Misses are traffic too

Two kinds of miss hurt more than ordinary ones:

- **Misses for things that don't exist.** A cache that only remembers hits
  sends every "user not found" to the database. Cache the absence, with a
  shorter TTL, like DNS does with NXDOMAIN (05).
- **Many misses for the same key at once.** A hot key expires and 500
  requests miss in the same millisecond: a *stampede*. Collapse them into
  one load and let everyone wait on it: *single-flight* (08).

```
 t0  get(k) ─┐
 t1  get(k) ─┼──► ONE loader call ──► every caller gets the same answer
 t2  get(k) ─┘
```

### 5 · Time is an input

A TTL cache that calls `System.currentTimeMillis()` can only be tested by
sleeping. Inject the clock (`LongSupplier`, `java.time.Clock`) and a test
can stand at t = 99 and t = 100 and check the boundary exactly. Every
exercise with time in it takes a `FakeClock` you move by hand.

## The details that bite

1. **Insertion order is not recency.** A plain `LinkedHashMap` is FIFO:
   reads move nothing and the hottest key goes first. Pass
   `accessOrder = true` (01).
2. **Replacing is not growing.** `put` on an existing key must not evict
   anyone, because the size did not change (01, 07).
3. **`<` versus `<=` at the expiry instant.** Store `expiresAt = put + ttl`
   and treat `now < expiresAt` as alive; at exactly `expiresAt` it is gone
   (02, 05, 06).
4. **A read does not extend a TTL** unless you deliberately chose
   "expire after access". Refreshing on get keeps a stale hot value alive
   forever (02).
5. **`size()` must not count the dead.** Lazy expiry leaves corpses in the
   map until someone touches them (02).
6. **Cache first, database second is backwards.** If the db write then
   fails, the cache serves a value that was never stored (03).
7. **An absent row is not a value.** Don't cache it by accident (03); cache
   it on purpose, with its own TTL, and overwrite it when the row is
   created (05).
8. **An exception is not "not found".** Caching a timeout turns a blip into
   a confident lie for every caller (04, 05).
9. **`0 / 0` is NaN.** `hitRate()` before the first request must be 0.0 (04).
10. **Dead entries leave before live ones are evicted.** A size eviction
    while an expired entry still holds a slot throws away a good value for
    nothing (06).
11. **Listener code is someone else's code.** Its exception must not
    abort the put halfway (06).
12. **LFU's minimum moves.** Promote the last key out of the lowest bucket
    and `minFreq` goes up; insert a new key and it drops back to 1 (07).
13. **Register cleanup after publishing.** `whenComplete` on an already
    completed future runs immediately, before your `put`. Order them the
    other way and the finished flight stays in the map forever (08).
14. **Never hand out the shared future.** Anyone holding a
    `CompletableFuture` can `complete` or `cancel` it for everyone; give
    each caller `copy()` (08).

## Where you will meet this

| idea | production form |
| --- | --- |
| LRU / LFU / TTL | Caffeine, Guava `CacheBuilder`, Redis `maxmemory-policy`, Memcached |
| read-through + stats | `LoadingCache`, Spring `@Cacheable`, Micrometer cache metrics |
| cache-aside | the default Redis pattern in front of SQL |
| negative caching | DNS NXDOMAIN TTL, CDN caching of 404s |
| removal listeners | Caffeine `RemovalListener`, closing pooled resources |
| single-flight | Go `singleflight`, Caffeine `AsyncLoadingCache`, CDN request collapsing |

Links forward: a cache absorbs load, but when the load still exceeds what
the backend can take, **10 · rate limits and resilience** decides who gets
turned away. Distributed caches shard keys with the hashing in **11**, and
invalidation across services travels as events in **12**. Module 08's
idempotent payments is the cousin of single-flight: both make a repeated
request take effect once.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-lru-cache.java` | ★☆☆ | an LRU cache on `LinkedHashMap` access order |
| 02 | `02-ttl-cache.java` | ★☆☆ | per-entry expiry with an injected clock and a purge |
| 03 | `03-write-policies.java` | ★★☆ | cache-aside vs write-through, including a failing db |
| 04 | `04-loading-cache.java` | ★★☆ | a read-through cache with hit/miss/load/eviction stats |
| 05 | `05-negative-caching.java` | ★★☆ | caching "not found" with its own TTL, but never errors |
| 06 | `06-removal-listener.java` | ★★☆ | TTL + LRU with removal causes and a safe listener |
| 07 | `07-lfu-cache.java` | ★★★ | O(1) LFU with frequency buckets and an LRU tie-break |
| 08 | `08-single-flight.java` | ★★★ | stampede protection: one load per key in flight |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/10-rate-limits-and-resilience`

javabootcamp/09-caching/01-lru-cache.instructions:
**Concepts:** LRU eviction · LinkedHashMap access order · bounded caches  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A cache is a small, fast map in front of something slow, and when it
is full it must forget something. LRU forgets the entry used longest
ago. Finish the nested class LruCache: get(key) returns an Optional
and a hit counts as a use; put(key, value) inserts or replaces (also a
use) and, only if the size now exceeds capacity, evicts the least
recently used key. A miss changes nothing. keysOldestFirst() returns a
copy of the keys from least to most recently used. A capacity below 1
is an IllegalArgumentException.

    cap 2: put a, put b, get a, put c   → b is evicted
    keysOldestFirst()                   → [a, c]
    cap 2 holding a, b: put(a, 9)       → nothing evicted, [b, a]

hint: LinkedHashMap has a constructor flag and a hook made for this.
javabootcamp/09-caching/01-lru-cache.explanation:
An LRU cache needs two things at once: O(1) lookup by key and an order
of "how recently was this used". A HashMap gives the first, a linked
list the second; LinkedHashMap is exactly that pair. Built with
accessOrder = true, every get and every put of an existing key moves
the entry to the tail, so the head is always the least recently used.
Overriding removeEldestEntry turns it into a bounded cache: put calls
it after inserting, and returning true drops the head.
The classic wrong turn is the default insertion order (FIFO): reads
never move anything, and the hottest key is the first one evicted.
The second is evicting BEFORE the put: replacing a key on a full cache
then throws away an innocent entry although the size never grows.
Java trap: inside the anonymous subclass, size() is the map's own
size, and capacity must be a final field (or effectively final local)
for the override to see it. keysOldestFirst returns a copy; handing
out keySet() would let callers remove entries behind the cache's back.

javabootcamp/09-caching/02-ttl-cache.instructions:
**Concepts:** TTL expiry · injected clock · lazy vs eager purge  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A session cache must not serve yesterday's data, so every entry gets
a time to live. Finish the nested class TtlCache. The clock is an
injected LongSupplier of milliseconds. An entry put at time t is alive
while now < t + ttl and dead from t + ttl on. get returns Optional and
does NOT extend the lifetime; a get that finds a dead entry removes
it. put on an existing key replaces it and restarts its lifetime.
size() counts live entries only; purgeExpired() removes every dead
entry and returns how many it removed. A ttl below 1 is an
IllegalArgumentException.

    ttl 100, put("k") at t=1000:   get at t=1099 → present
                                   get at t=1100 → empty

hint: store when the entry dies, not when it was born.
javabootcamp/09-caching/02-ttl-cache.explanation:
Store the moment an entry dies, not the moment it was born: with
expiresAt = now + ttl, "is it alive?" is one comparison, now <
expiresAt, and the boundary is unambiguous. At exactly expiresAt the
entry is dead, so it lived for ttl milliseconds, not ttl + 1.
Expiry here is lazy: get notices a dead entry and removes it, and
purgeExpired sweeps the rest (a real cache runs that sweep on a timer
or piggybacks it on writes). size() must not count corpses, so it
filters by the same alive() rule rather than returning map.size().
The wrong turns: refreshing expiresAt on get (that is "expire after
access", a different policy, and it keeps a hot stale value alive
forever); using <= so entries live one millisecond too long; and
reading System.currentTimeMillis() directly, which makes every test
either slow (sleep) or flaky. Injecting the clock as a LongSupplier
is what lets the tests jump to t = 99 and t = 100 exactly.
values().removeIf deletes in place without a
ConcurrentModificationException; counting first gives the return.

javabootcamp/09-caching/03-write-policie.instructions:
**Concepts:** cache-aside · write-through · invalidation · failure order  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Two ways to keep a cache in front of a database. Both READ the same
way: a cache hit returns it; a miss reads the db and caches the row if
there is one (an absent row is never cached). They WRITE differently:
  CacheAside.write    → db.write, then REMOVE the key from the cache
  WriteThrough.write  → db.write, then PUT the value in the cache
The db always goes first: if db.write throws, the exception propagates
and the cache is left exactly as it was. Finish read and cached in
CachedStore and write in both subclasses; cached(key) shows what the
cache holds without touching the db.

    cache-aside:   read u1, write(u1, grace) → cached(u1) → empty
    write-through: write(u2, linus)          → cached(u2) → linus

hint: ask what the cache holds if the second line of write never runs.
javabootcamp/09-caching/03-write-policie.explanation:
Both stores read the same way (look in the cache, on a miss load from
the database and remember the row), so the read lives in one shared
helper. They differ only in what a write does to the cache:
  cache-aside   — db.write, then cache.remove: the next read reloads.
  write-through — db.write, then cache.put: the next read is a hit.
Cache-aside deletes instead of updating because a delete can never
install a WRONG value: if two writers race, "set" can leave the older
value cached forever, while "delete" at worst costs one extra load.
Write-through pays a cache write on every db write, even for keys
nobody reads, in exchange for warm reads.
The order is the whole exercise. The database is the source of truth,
so it goes first; if it throws, the exception propagates before the
cache is touched, and cache and db still agree. Cache-first is the
classic bug: the db write fails and the cache now serves a value that
was never stored. An absent row is not cached (a later insert would be
hidden); exercise 05 shows how to cache misses deliberately.

javabootcamp/09-caching/04-loading-cache.instructions:
**Concepts:** read-through loading · hit rate · eviction counts · LRU  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Callers should not care whether a value came from the cache: they call
get(key), and on a miss the cache itself calls the loader and keeps
the result. Finish the nested class LoadingCache (LRU-bounded, like
01). Every get is exactly one hit or one miss. loads counts loader
calls that returned a value; evictions counts entries dropped for
capacity. If the loader throws, the exception propagates; if it
returns null, throw IllegalStateException; either way nothing is
cached. invalidate(key) removes a key and is NOT an eviction.
hitRate() = hits / (hits + misses), and 0.0 before any request.
A capacity below 1 is an IllegalArgumentException.

    cap 2: get a, get a        → stats (hits 1, misses 1, loads 1, ev 0)
    get a x4                   → hitRate 0.75

hint: count the hit or miss before you call the loader.
javabootcamp/09-caching/04-loading-cache.explanation:
Read-through moves the "on a miss, load and remember" logic from every
caller into the cache itself: callers just say get(key), and the
loader is the only code that knows about the slow backend. That is the
shape of Guava's LoadingCache and Caffeine's get(key, loader).
The stats are what make a cache operable. A dashboard shows hitRate;
if it is 0.2 the cache is mostly overhead, and a rising evictions
count says the capacity is too small for the working set.
The counting rules: every get is exactly one hit or one miss, decided
before the loader runs; loads counts only loads that produced a value,
so a failing backend shows up as misses without loads. A loader that
throws or returns null caches NOTHING: caching an exception would turn
one hiccup into an outage for that key, and null is not a value.
invalidate is a deliberate removal, not an eviction, so it is not
counted: evictions measures capacity pressure only.
hitRate guards the 0 / 0 case; (double) hits / requests with 0
requests is NaN, which then poisons every average it touches.
Eviction reuses the LinkedHashMap access-order trick from exercise 01,
with the counter bumped inside removeEldestEntry.

javabootcamp/09-caching/05-negative-cach.instructions:
**Concepts:** negative caching · two TTLs · errors vs absence · TTL  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Lookups for things that don't exist are the ones a plain cache never
helps with. Finish the nested class NegativeCache. find(key) answers
from a live cache entry, otherwise asks the backend and caches its
answer: a found value for positiveTtl, an empty Optional ("not found")
for negativeTtl. Entries are alive while now < storedAt + ttl. If the
backend throws, the exception propagates and nothing is cached.
onCreated(key, value) caches a value the system just created (for
positiveTtl), replacing a remembered miss. invalidate(key) drops any
entry. A ttl below 1 is an IllegalArgumentException.

    positive 1000, negative 100:
    find(bob) at t=0 → empty (backend asked)   at t=99 → empty (cached)
    find(bob) at t=100                         → backend asked again

hint: the cached thing can be the Optional itself.
javabootcamp/09-caching/05-negative-cach.explanation:
A cache that only remembers hits is useless against the most expensive
traffic: lookups for things that do not exist (a scraper probing
random ids, a typo'd username refreshed in a loop). Every one of them
falls through to the database. DNS solved this decades ago: an
NXDOMAIN answer is cached too, with its own, shorter TTL.
So the entry stores the Optional itself, present or empty, plus its
expiry, and the TTL is picked by which one it is. The negative TTL is
shorter because absence is the answer most likely to change: someone
signs up with that name a second later.
That is also why onCreated exists. Without it, a freshly created user
is "not found" for up to negativeTtl after signing up; writing the new
value straight into the cache overwrites the remembered miss.
The trap is treating an exception as absence. "The database timed
out" is not "the user does not exist"; caching it would turn a blip
into a confident lie for every caller. Exceptions propagate, nothing
is stored, and the next find asks again.
Expiry follows exercise 02: alive while now < expiresAt.

javabootcamp/09-caching/06-removal-liste.instructions:
**Concepts:** removal callbacks · eviction causes · TTL + size · isolation  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Finish ListeningCache: LRU, at most capacity entries, each alive while
now < putTime + ttl. Every removal calls listener.onRemoval(key,
value, cause) with the value that left:
  get of a dead entry            → removes it, EXPIRED, returns empty
  invalidate                     → EXPLICIT if alive, EXPIRED if dead,
                                   nothing if absent
  put over an existing key       → old value REPLACED if alive,
                                   EXPIRED if dead
  put that overflows capacity    → first EVERY dead entry leaves
    (EXPIRED, least recently used first); then, if still too many,
    least recently used live entries leave (SIZE); a put that fits
    leaves dead entries where they are
get hits and puts count as uses. A listener that throws a
RuntimeException must not break the cache: count it (listenerErrors).

    cap 2: put a, put b, get a, put c   → [b=2 SIZE]

hint: route every removal through one private notify method.
javabootcamp/09-caching/06-removal-liste.explanation:
Caches that hold resources (open files, pooled connections, rendered
images) need to know when an entry leaves so they can close it, and
operators want to know WHY: lots of SIZE evictions means the cache is
too small, lots of EXPIRED means the TTL is short, REPLACED means hot
keys are being rewritten. Caffeine's RemovalCause has these four,
plus COLLECTED for entries lost to weak or soft references.
Every exit path goes through one notify method, so no path can forget
to report. The interesting rules are in put:
1. An old entry for the same key is REPLACED only if it was still
   alive; a dead one was already gone, so it is reported EXPIRED.
2. When the cache overflows, dead entries leave first. Evicting a live
   entry for SIZE while a corpse still occupies a slot throws away a
   useful value for nothing (a pure-LRU sweep makes exactly that
   mistake when the corpse was recently read).
3. Only then, if still too big, evict least recently used. The entry
   just written is the most recently used, so it never goes.
Listener code is someone else's code. If its exception escaped, a put
would fail halfway (entry stored, eviction skipped) and the cache would
stay over capacity. So notify catches RuntimeException, counts it, and
moves on; Caffeine does the same and logs it.

javabootcamp/09-caching/07-lfu-cache.instructions:
**Concepts:** LFU eviction · frequency buckets · LRU tie-break · O(1)  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

LRU forgets a key used 1000 times the moment a scan walks past it; LFU
keeps what is used often. Finish the nested class LfuCache. A new key
starts at frequency 1; every get hit and every put on an existing key
(which replaces the value, evicting nothing) adds 1. When put brings a
NEW key into a full cache, first evict the key with the lowest
frequency; among equals, the one least recently used (got or put).
frequency(key) is 0 for an absent key, and an evicted key forgets its
count. A capacity below 1 is an IllegalArgumentException.

    cap 2: put a, put b, get a, put c         → b evicted (1 < 2)
    cap 2: put a, put b, get b, get a, put c  → b evicted (tie, older use)

Aim for O(1) per operation (the tests don't time it).
hint: group keys by frequency, and remember the smallest group.
javabootcamp/09-caching/07-lfu-cache.explanation:
LRU is fooled by a scan: one pass over a million cold keys flushes
every hot key. LFU keeps what is used OFTEN, which survives scans; the
price is that frequency must be tracked and ties must be broken.
The O(1) design keeps three maps: key → value, key → frequency, and
frequency → LinkedHashSet of keys with that frequency, in the order
they reached it. A use moves the key from bucket f to the TAIL of
bucket f + 1, so the head of each bucket is that bucket's least
recently used key. minFreq names the lowest non-empty bucket, so the
victim is always buckets.get(minFreq).iterator().next().
minFreq is where the bugs live. When a use empties the minFreq bucket,
minFreq goes up by exactly one (the key just moved there). A brand
new key resets minFreq to 1, even if every other key is hotter: the
newcomer is now the coldest thing in the cache, and the next newcomer
evicts it. That is LFU's known weakness (new keys struggle to stay);
real systems use aging or W-TinyLFU's admission window.
Eviction happens BEFORE inserting the new key, otherwise the newcomer
(frequency 1, most recent) could be chosen as its own victim. Evicted
keys forget their history: coming back means starting at 1.

javabootcamp/09-caching/08-single-flight.instructions:
**Concepts:** cache stampede · single-flight · CompletableFuture · cleanup  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A hot key expires and hundreds of requests miss at once. Finish
SingleFlight so that while a load for a key is running ("in flight"),
further get(key) calls do NOT call the loader again but wait for the
same result. When the flight completes (value or exception) it is
forgotten: the next get starts a new load, and failures are shared by
all waiters but never remembered. This includes a loader whose future
is already complete when it returns. Each caller gets its OWN future:
cancelling or completing it must not affect the flight or the other
callers. inFlight() counts keys with a load running.

    get(k), get(k)            → loader called once, inFlight() → 1
    backend finishes k        → both futures → "row k", inFlight() → 0

The tests complete the backend's futures by hand: no threads, no sleep.
hint: CompletableFuture.copy() exists, and when whenComplete runs matters.
javabootcamp/09-caching/08-single-flight.explanation:
A hot key expires and 500 requests miss at the same instant; without
coordination all 500 hit the database for the same row (a "cache
stampede" or "dog-pile"). Single-flight, named after Go's
golang.org/x/sync/singleflight, lets the first caller start the load
and makes everyone who arrives while it is running wait on the same
result. It is not a cache: once the flight lands the entry is gone,
and the cache in front of it stores the value.
The map holds the one shared future per key. Two details make it
correct:
1. Cleanup is registered AFTER the put. whenComplete on an already
   completed future runs immediately, so registering it first would
   remove nothing and then the put would leave a finished flight in
   the map forever: every later get would return the stale result.
   remove(key, fresh) only removes that exact flight.
2. Every caller gets fresh.copy(), not fresh. A CompletableFuture is
   writable by whoever holds it; hand out the shared one and a single
   caller's cancel() or complete(...) decides the answer for all.
Failures are shared too (each waiter sees the same exception) and are
never remembered, so the next get starts a new flight. Java trap:
doing this inside HashMap.computeIfAbsent breaks when the cleanup runs
synchronously, because the map is modified during its own compute.
